verdict.rationale: The phrase 'a thousand years' (chilia ete, made of G5507 plus G2094) appears as a defined unit only in Revelation 20:2-7, six times across six verses, and nowhere else in either Testament. The verb 'they lived' or 'they came to life' (ezesan, a completed past action of zao G2198) is used for one group on thrones in 20:4 and again of the rest of the dead in 20:5, with 'the first resurrection' (anastasis he prote, G0386) as the lexical hinge. Three readings are defensible from the words. A sequential reading takes 'they lived' (ezesan) in one bodily sense both times and places Christ's return (chapter 19) before the reign. A non-bodily reading takes the 'souls' (psychas) of 20:4 as enthroned regenerate or martyred saints and 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) as a symbolic span of the present age. A triumphalist reading takes 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) as a long figurative gospel epoch culminating in the return. The Greek of Revelation 20 nowhere uses 'coming' or 'presence' (parousia) or any return-vocabulary at the start of the thousand years, and the wider canon supplies symbolic numerics (Revelation 11:3, 12:6, 14:20; 2 Peter 3:8) on the one hand and concrete day-of-the-LORD imagery (Zechariah 14; Isaiah 11; Isaiah 65) on the other without ranking them. The verdict held is therefore disputed at the lexical level, on the same footing as amillennialism.

scripture.reasoning: An angel 'binds' (edesen, a completed past action of deo G1210) the dragon, who is named the ancient serpent and the devil and Satan, for 'a thousand years' (chilia ete, G5507 plus G2094). This is the first of six occurrences of the bounded phrase 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) in Revelation 20:2-7, and the only place in the canon where the phrase is a defined block. The verb 'to bind' (deo) is the same verb used of binding the strong man in Matthew 12:29 and Mark 3:27, which is the lexical link by which a non-future reading takes Satan's binding as already accomplished in Christ's first-advent ministry rather than as a future epoch.

Satan is cast into the 'abyss' (abyssos G0012) and sealed so that he will not 'deceive' (planao G4105) the nations until the 'thousand years' (chilia ete) are 'completed' (telesthe, a completed past passive action of teleo, meaning 'to bring to an end'). The verb 'to deceive' (planao) is used across the whole Bible (pan-canonically, meaning spread across the whole Bible) of end-times deception (Matthew 24:4-5, 24; 2 Timothy 3:13; Revelation 12:9; 13:14; 19:20). Whether the present age is one in which Satan is bound from totally deceiving the nations or not is the precise point on which lexical data is genuinely silent, since the sealing clause states only the duration and the purpose, not the absolute extent of restriction.

John sees thrones and 'souls' (psychas) of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus, and 'they lived' or 'they came to life' (ezesan, a completed past action of zao G2198) plus 'they reigned' (ebasileusan, a completed past action of basileuo G0936) with Christ 'a thousand years' (chilia ete). The verb 'to live' (zao) occurs 143 times in the Greek New Testament and carries both bodily senses (John 11:25; Revelation 1:18 of Christ alive after death) and non-bodily senses (Romans 6:11 alive to God; Galatians 2:20; Hebrews 12:9). The explicit grammatical subject is 'souls' (psychas), which a non-bodily reading takes as decisive against physical resurrection here and a literal reading explains as a 'synecdoche' (a figure where a part stands for the whole) for whole persons. Neither grammar alone nor the noun 'souls' (psychas) alone forecloses the other reading.

The rest of the dead 'did not live' (ouk ezesan, same verb as v.4) until the 'thousand years' (chilia ete) were completed. This is 'the first resurrection' (anastasis he prote, G0386). The lexical hinge is whether the identical verb 'they lived' (ezesan) bears the same sense in both clauses. If it does (the standard lexical principle of consistent sense within an adjacent parallel), the second group's coming-to-life is bodily, which forces the first group's to be bodily as well, yielding two bodily resurrections. If verse 4 is non-bodily and verse 5 is bodily, the parallel is broken by an unstated shift. The label 'the first resurrection' (anastasis he prote) distinguishes a first from a second, which the pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) use of 'resurrection' (anastasis, 42 occurrences, dominantly bodily: John 11:24; Acts 4:33; 1 Corinthians 15) inclines toward a bodily reading, but the Revelation context permits a figurative one.

Blessed and holy is the one having part in the 'first resurrection' (anastasis G0386), over whom the second death has no authority; they will be priests of God and of Christ and 'they shall reign' (basileusousin, future tense of basileuo G0936) with him 'a thousand years' (chilia ete). The pairing of first resurrection with escape from the second death is read by a future-bodily lens as marking a raised company before a later judgment, and by a present-spiritual lens as the regenerate soul secure in the in-between state. The clause does not name the 'coming' or 'presence' (parousia) and does not lexically locate Christ's return at the start of the thousand years.

When the 'thousand years' (chilia ete) are completed, Satan will be 'released' (luthesetai, future of luo G3089, meaning 'to loose') from his prison. The verb 'to loose' (luo) is the lexical inverse of 'he bound' (edesen, G1210) in 20:2; binding and loosing frame the thousand-year block as a bounded interval. The verbs themselves are ordinary lexical items and do not specify whether the interval is a literal thousand years or a symbolic span.

With the Lord one day is as 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) and 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) as one day. This is the only place outside Revelation 20 where the bounded phrase 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) appears, and it appears explicitly as a symbolic equivalence with one day ('as a single day,' hos hemera mia, with the particle 'as' (hos) signaling figurative comparison). The verse does not say the Revelation 20 thousand years is symbolic, but it shows the same vocabulary used elsewhere by an apostle in an explicitly symbolic way, which is the lexical warrant for the non-literal reading.

The two witnesses prophesy 'one thousand two hundred sixty days' (chilias diakosias hexekonta hemeras). Three other Revelation uses of 'thousands' (chilioi: here, 12:6, 14:20) appear in compound numbers that are widely taken as symbolic time spans or symbolic measures. This shows that Revelation itself uses 'thousands' (chilioi) within figurative numerical schemes, which is the in-book lexical warrant for reading 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) in Revelation 20:2-7 symbolically rather than literally.

His feet shall 'stand' (amad H5975) on the Mount of Olives, which splits, 'half' (chatsi, H2677) toward east and 'half' (chatsi) toward west. The text describes a God-appearing (theophanic) day of the LORD with concrete topography but assigns no thousand-year duration and gives no sequence relative to any resurrection. The half-and-half splitting ('half,' chatsi) is geographic, not temporal, so it cannot by itself supply a thousand-year timetable.

The LORD shall 'be' (hayah H1961) 'king' (melek H4428) over all the earth, the LORD 'one' (echad H0259) and his name 'one' (echad). This universal kingship is lexically open as to whether it denotes a discrete future earthly reign of fixed length or the completed reign of God without a thousand-year interim. The verse supplies kingship but not chronology.

The 'wolf' (zeeb H2061) shall 'dwell' (gur H1481) with the 'lamb' (kebes H3532), describing a peaceful order. The imagery is read by a future-earthly view as conditions of a coming earthly reign and by a realized view as the redeemed order begun in Christ. The vocabulary is descriptive of harmony, not of a thousand-year span, so it neither dates nor demands a literal thousand years.

No more shall there be in it an infant that lives only a few days, nor an old man who does not fill out his days, for the youth shall 'die' (mut H4191) 'a hundred years old' (shanah H8141, meaning 'year'). The text pictures an era in which 'death' (mut) is still present yet abnormal, which a future-earthly reading takes as a key lexical anchor: it cannot be the new heavens and new earth of Revelation 21:4 where death is no more, so it must denote an in-between era. A figurative reading takes the vocabulary as overstated ('hyperbolic') blessing imagery for the new creation itself. The presence of 'death' (mut) in the end-times vision is the lexical pressure point.

The disciples ask whether at this time he will 'restore' (apokathistemi G0600) the kingdom to Israel. The verb 'to restore' (apokathistemi) denotes restoration to a former state. Christ's reply in v.7 redirects to times and seasons hidden in the Father's authority without denying the category of the question. The literal reading takes the unrebuked question as preserving the expectation of an earthly Israel-centered restoration that the post-coming ('after the parousia') thousand years answers. A non-literal reading takes the kingdom restoration as fulfilled in the Spirit-empowered church (v.8). The verb itself is lexically neutral on chronology.

Each in his own 'order' or 'rank' (idios tagma, G5001): Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his 'coming' (en te parousia, G3952). The noun 'rank' or 'order' (tagma) is a 'hapax' (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament here) and means rank or order. Paul names two 'ranks' (tagma plural sense), Christ then his people, both tied to the 'coming' (parousia). The lexical question is whether 'rank' (tagma) admits more ranks (a third group after a gap, hence a future earthly era between Christ's people and the end) or only the two named. Paul's wording does not lexically exclude a further rank but does not name one either, so the text is genuinely underdetermined on this point.

All who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth, those who did good to 'a resurrection of life' (anastasis zoes) and those who did evil to 'a resurrection of judgment' (anastasis kriseos). The single sentence describes a single hour (v.28) with two outcomes within one resurrection event named 'resurrection' (anastasis). This is the single-resurrection pattern in lexically explicit form. The literal reading of Revelation 20 must reconcile this single hour with two resurrections separated by 'a thousand years' (chilia ete), either by treating John's hour as compressed prophetic language or by reading the second outcome as the second-stage resurrection. The texts together are not flatly contradictory but they are also not flatly harmonized at the word level.

complicating_texts.resolution: The single verb 'they lived' (ezesan, G2198) governs both the company of v.4 and the rest of the dead in v.5. A sequential reading insists the verb cannot shift sense within two adjacent clauses, so both denote bodily coming-to-life, yielding two resurrections separated by 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) and a future reign. A non-bodily reading observes that v.4 names the subjects as 'souls' (psychas) and sets the action among heavenly thrones, permitting a different sense for the first group (entrance into heavenly life or enthronement) while the second group's clause concerns physical raising at the end. Lexicography (the study of word meanings) does not adjudicate the parallel principle versus the noun-souls ('psychas') restriction, so the complication is recognized as genuinely unresolved at the word level and drives the disputed verdict rather than being dissolved by it.

The noun 'souls' (psychas) as the explicit subject of 'they lived' (ezesan) is the chief complication for a straightforward bodily reading. If souls are the ones who lived and reigned, the coming-to-life may describe disembodied life or enthronement rather than physical resurrection, undercutting a clean two-bodily-resurrection scheme. The literal reading answers that 'souls' (psychas) can stand for whole persons by 'synecdoche' (a figure where a part stands for the whole) and that the following reign vocabulary presupposes embodiment. Both moves are lexically permissible. The complication is acknowledged but cannot be lexically dissolved.

Christ teaches a single hour in which all in the tombs hear his voice and come forth to two destinies, 'a resurrection of life' (anastasis zoes) and 'a resurrection of judgment' (anastasis kriseos). This single-event two-outcome pattern is the textually clearest New Testament resurrection schema and uses the same noun 'resurrection' (anastasis, G0386) Revelation 20 uses. A literal Revelation 20 reading must say John 5 collapses a temporally separated pair into a prophetic horizon, or that the second outcome there is the same as the second resurrection of Revelation 20:5. The reconciliation is possible but is not on the surface of either text. Recorded here as addressed but unresolved at the word level.

Paul orders the resurrection as Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his 'coming' (parousia, G3952), and then the 'end' (telos, v.24). The vocabulary names two 'ranks' (tagma G5001, a hapax meaning a word that occurs only once in the New Testament) plus a final completion. The text does not name a third 'rank' (tagma) between 'coming' (parousia) and 'end' (telos), which is the lexical pressure against a separate post-coming thousand-year era containing additional events. A literal-thousand-year reading takes the 'thousand years' (chilia ete) to fall inside the implied gap between v.23's 'coming' (parousia) and v.24's 'end' (telos); a non-thousand-year reading takes 'coming' (parousia) and 'end' (telos) as the same event. Lexically the text is silent on which.

Isaiah's vision contains the verb 'to die' (mut, H4191) in the end-times state, which is incompatible with the Revelation 21:4 promise that there will be no more death. A future-earthly reading uses this incompatibility as a lexical wedge for an in-between era still touched by mortality (the thousand years). A figurative reading takes the language as overstated ('hyperbolic') blessing imagery within new-creation discourse rather than a literal description of conditions. The wedge is lexically real but does not by itself name the duration of any in-between era.

Peter explicitly uses 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) in a symbolic equivalence: with the Lord one day is as 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) and 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) as one day. The particle 'as' (hos) marks the comparison as figurative. This is the only non-Revelation use of the bounded phrase in the canon, and it shows the same vocabulary functioning symbolically in apostolic teaching. A literal-thousand-year reading replies that one symbolic use elsewhere does not force a symbolic use here, especially since 2 Peter is comparing temporal scale generally; a non-literal reading replies that the apostolic precedent shows the phrase carries no automatic literal sense. Addressed; lexically underdetermined.

variants.note: Revelation is outside the CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method) 3 John sample, so no ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) was consulted. The Nestle-Aland sigla (standard reference marks for variant readings) visible in the supplied Greek of Revelation 20 mark minor word-order and morphological (word-form) variants around 'a thousand years' (chilia ete), 'they lived' (ezesan), and the verbs of binding and loosing; none of them shifts the lexical pressure point of whether 'they lived' (ezesan) means bodily resurrection or whether 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) is literal. The verdict does not turn on any variant unit.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the chronological flow of Revelation 19 to 20 as sequential: Christ returns on the white horse in chapter 19, then in chapter 20 Satan is bound and the 'thousand years' (chilia ete) begin. Takes both occurrences of 'they lived' (ezesan, G2198) in 20:4-5 in the same bodily sense, so 'the first resurrection' (anastasis he prote, G0386) is the bodily raising of the saints before the 'thousand years' (chilia ete) and the rest are raised bodily after, with 'to reign' (basileuo, G0936) a real reign. Adds the lexical pressure of Isaiah 65:20 (death still present), Acts 1:6 (restoration to Israel not denied), and the unrebuked disciple question for an in-between earthly era. The position is strongest where it lets the standard sense of bodily-resurrection vocabulary stand in the most explicit thousand-year passage.

Takes 'they lived' (ezesan) in v.4 as the heavenly life or enthronement of 'souls' ('psychas' explicit subject) and the first resurrection as regeneration or the saints' entry into the in-between state, with 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) as a symbolic figure for the entire between-the-comings age. Cites the symbolic numerics across Revelation (Revelation 11:3, 12:6, 14:20) and the explicit symbolic use of 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) in 2 Peter 3:8, the single-resurrection pattern of John 5:28-29 (one hour, two destinies under one 'resurrection,' anastasis), and the absence of 'coming' (parousia) vocabulary in Revelation 20. On this reading there is no future post-coming earthly thousand years and Christ returns once to the final judgment. The position is strongest where it lets the consistent New Testament pattern of one 'coming' (parousia) and one bodily resurrection event control the figurative numerics of an apocalyptic (highly symbolic prophetic) chapter.

Treats 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) as a long symbolic period of gospel triumph within history that precedes Christ's return, so Christ comes after, not before, the thousand-year flourishing. The verbs 'to reign' (basileuo) and 'they lived' (ezesan) are read as the spiritual reign of the saints expanding in the present age, with Satan bound from preventing the gospel's progress to the nations. Cites the Matthew 12:29 binding of the strong man ('to bind,' deo, G1210) as already accomplished in Christ. The position is strongest where it lets the kingdom growth motifs of the Gospels and the worldwide vocabulary of the Great Commission control the timing of the 'coming' (parousia).

hermeneutics.notes: The dispute is structural and lexical at once. The decisive question is whether the single verb 'they lived' (ezesan) carries one sense across Revelation 20:4-5 and whether 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) is literal or symbolic. Revelation's own pattern of symbolic numerics (1260 days, 144000, the sevens) sits alongside the chronological flow of chapters 19 to 20 that reads naturally as sequential. The Old Testament anchors (Zechariah 14, Isaiah 11, Isaiah 65, Romans 11) supply kingship and restoration vocabulary and one explicit anomaly (death in Isaiah 65:20) but no chronology that fixes a return before a thousand-year span. 'Scripture interpreting scripture' (analogia scripturae) yields the symbolic 2 Peter 3:8 use of 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) on one side and the single-resurrection John 5:28-29 pattern on one side, against the natural sequential reading of Revelation 19-20 on the other. The lexicon does not break the tie.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The relationship between the return of Christ, a thousand-year reign, and the present age, as that relationship is expressed in Revelation 20:1-7 and related texts.
stem_audit.notes: VERDICT-CHANGED: The original stem encodes a pre-thousand-year sequence by asserting Christ returns before a literal thousand-year reign that is future and distinct from the present age. That phrasing presupposes a literal reading of 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) and a particular ordering of the 'coming' (parousia) relative to the thousand years, which are the very points in dispute. The verdict is derived on the original stem; the neutralized form is recorded so the lexical contest, whether the thousand years is literal and whether the return precedes it, is visible without the wording prejudging it. Held to disputed at low confidence, the same lexical footing as the amillennialism and postmillennialism judgments, because the words underdetermine (do not settle) the thousand-year scheme.

lay_summary: This proposition stands or falls almost entirely on six verses, Revelation 20:1-7, with supporting glances at Zechariah 14, Isaiah 11, Isaiah 65, Romans 11, and Acts 1. The Greek phrase 'a thousand years' (chilia ete) is a defined unit only in those six verses of Revelation 20, and apart from one passage in 2 Peter where it is used in a deliberately figurative way (one day as a thousand years), the phrase does not appear in the rest of the Bible. So the entire thousand-year scheme rests on one symbolic-prophetic block. Inside that block, two things have to be decided from the words on the page. First, the verb 'they lived' or 'they came to life' (ezesan) appears once for a group on thrones in verse 4 and again for the rest of the dead in verse 5. One reading holds that the same verb means the same thing both times, namely a bodily raising, so there are two bodily resurrections separated by a thousand years, which is named 'the first resurrection' (anastasis he prote). On that reading the return of the King comes first and a real earthly reign follows. A second reading notes that the ones who come to life in verse 4 are called 'souls' (psychas) and are pictured among heavenly thrones, which allows that first coming-to-life to mean entrance into heavenly life rather than a body leaving a grave. On that reading the thousand years is a symbolic span covering the whole present age. A third reading takes the thousand years as a long figurative epoch of gospel flourishing within history, before the return. Second, the number itself, a thousand, can be a literal count or a symbol of fullness. Revelation elsewhere uses thousands in symbolic numerical schemes (1260 days, 144000, the seven sevens), and Peter uses the same words in an explicitly figurative way, both of which weigh toward symbolism. The Old Testament anchors describe a coming day when the LORD reigns as king over all the earth and a peaceable order where wolf and lamb lie down together, and one passage in Isaiah 65 mentions death still happening in that era, which is the strongest single text for an in-between era distinct from the final new creation. But none of these passages attaches a fixed length to the reign or dates it before or after any specific resurrection event. Because each reading is defensible from the words on the page and the text supplies no lexical hinge that settles the order or the duration, the honest finding is that the pattern is contested rather than plainly for or against.
